name: Chlorhexidine mouthwash

lead: Chlorhexidine mouthwash is an antiseptic rinse used alongside brushing to cut plaque and calm gum inflammation. People use it for healthier gums and a fresher mouth, and it is often the comparison rinse in trials of other mouthwashes.

It is a cationic antiseptic that binds to teeth, gums and bacterial membranes, leaving a lingering antibacterial effect. It is one of the most studied antiplaque agents, has been used in medicine since the 1950s, is on the WHO Essential Medicines List, and is also used in hospitals, for example in oral care for ventilated patients.

paras: It is a pharmacy or prescription rinse used after brushing for a limited period, such as during a gum flare-up or after dental work. Many people alternate it with a regular rinse rather than using it continuously.

Common effects are brown tooth staining after a month or more, taste disturbance and a dry or irritated mouth; allergic reactions are rare. Labels advise limiting use to about six months, and a 2020 study found a week of use shifted the oral microbiome.

angle.text: Chlorhexidine rinse is used alongside brushing to cut plaque and gum inflammation, giving healthier gums and a fresher mouth. It is among the best-studied antiplaque rinses, with tooth staining and taste change documented as accompanying effects.

lead: Chlorhexidine mouthwash is an antiseptic oral rinse, generally in the 0.05 to 0.2 percent range, used alongside toothbrushing to reduce dental plaque and gingivitis [1][2]. In appearance terms, people use it to keep gums calm and less inflamed, to lower the bacterial load behind bad breath, and to protect the look of the gumline during periods such as orthodontic treatment or after oral procedures [2][3][4].

Chlorhexidine came into medical use in the 1950s and is on the World Health Organization Essential Medicines List [2]. It is one of the most studied antiplaque agents, and it has also been trialled in hospital settings, including prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia, management of oral mucositis in cancer patients and decolonisation of MRSA carriers [5][6][7][8].

The best-known trade-off is cosmetic: with weeks of regular use, rinses can leave brown extrinsic stains on teeth and an altered taste, and manufacturers have developed anti-discoloration formulations in response [2][9][10]. Other documented effects include allergic reactions, and the US FDA label advises limiting use of the mouthwash to six months [2].
infobox: Prescription or over the counter depending on country and strength
FDA advises mouthwash use of no more than six months [2]

paras: Chlorhexidine entered medical use in the 1950s; Wikipedia cites a 1954 patent from I.C.I. and describes its structure as two biguanide units linked by a hexamethylene spacer.[2] In the late 1960s, Harald Loe showed that it could prevent plaque accumulation, which led to its development as an oral rinse.[1] It is now used far beyond dentistry: as a surgical skin antiseptic (Wikipedia reports it is considered more effective than povidone-iodine for clean surgery), for wound cleaning, for keeping urinary catheters from blocking, and for umbilical cord care, where a 2015 Cochrane review linked it to fewer cases of omphalitis.[2] It is on the World Health Organization Essential Medicines List and is sold under brands such as Peridex, Corsodyl, Hibiclens and ChloraPrep.[2]

Chlorhexidine rinses are used alongside normal tooth cleaning to reduce plaque and mild gingivitis; evidence is described as insufficient for moderate to severe gingivitis [2]. Chlorhexidine gel is also used after tooth extraction to lower dry-socket incidence, and the compound is used for root canal irrigation [2]. Reviews compare essential oil mouthwashes and oil pulling against it for plaque and gingival inflammation [11][12].

In orthodontic patients, fixed appliances make cleaning harder and gingivitis common. A 2022 systematic review of randomised trials covered 14 studies and 602 patients aged 11 to 35 using 0.06, 0.12 or 0.2 percent chlorhexidine rinses; it reported reduced plaque and gingival inflammation during treatment, with some comparison rinses deemed equally effective [3].

Cochrane reviews examined oral hygiene care, including chlorhexidine rinses, for preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia in critically ill patients [5][8]. A 2023 meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials with 657 patients reported that toothbrushing plus 0.2 or 0.12 percent chlorhexidine was associated with lower pneumonia incidence than chlorhexidine alone or brushing with placebo, and similar to cotton-wipe application of chlorhexidine [13].

A systematic review of basic oral care for oral mucositis in cancer patients and a 1994 randomised trial in radiation-induced mucositis also examined chlorhexidine rinses [6][14]. A New England Journal of Medicine trial assessed chlorhexidine mouthwash, with chlorhexidine bathing and nasal mupirocin, as decolonisation of MRSA carriers after hospital discharge [7].

Wikipedia's bad breath article says most genuine halitosis starts in the mouth, usually at the back of the tongue, where bacteria break down proteins and release volatile sulfur compounds such as hydrogen sulfide and methyl mercaptan; gum disease is another common contributor.[15] It lists tongue cleaning, mouthwash and flossing as usual first steps and says mouthwashes containing chlorhexidine or cetylpyridinium chloride have tentative evidence of benefit while both can temporarily stain teeth.[15] A 2024 editorial discussed chlorhexidine mouthwash and halitosis in surgical patients alongside its risks.[4] The same article describes bad breath as socially stigmatised and associated with anxiety, which is part of why breath care features in appearance-minded routines.[15]

sections.h: Formulations and how people use them
paras: As a mouthwash, chlorhexidine digluconate is used at 0.05 to 0.2 percent. Wikipedia's mouthwash article says there is no evidence that higher concentrations control plaque and gingivitis better, and describes a randomised trial in Rabat, Morocco, that found better plaque inhibition with an alcohol-based 0.12 percent rinse than with an alcohol-free 0.1 percent one.[1] Chlorhexidine also comes as a gel used after tooth extraction, and some products add chelated zinc or an anti-discoloration system to reduce staining.[2][10]

Product guidance is generally that the rinse is swished for about half a minute and spat out, and that it be used apart from brushing because anionic ingredients such as sodium lauryl sulfate in some toothpastes can reduce its activity; Wikipedia says to wait at least 30 minutes after other dental products.[1][2] A 2010 T Nation thread, includes a poster asking whether others have used chlorhexidine mouthwash after receiving a prescription bottle from a dentist.[16]

Extrinsic tooth staining can appear after four weeks or more of rinse use, and users may notice a bitter or metallic taste that Wikipedia says is made worse by rinsing with water afterward [2]. Formulations with chelated zinc are reported to stain less [2]. Other listed effects include allergic reactions, mouth lining irritation, tartar buildup, and eye damage on direct contact [2]. Chlorhexidine is ototoxic if it reaches the middle ear through a ruptured eardrum, and one case of fatal aspiration has been reported [2].
The FDA label advises limiting mouthwash use to six months [2]. Ingestion is poorly absorbed but can cause stomach irritation or nausea [2].

At physiological pH, chlorhexidine salts release a positively charged molecule that binds to negatively charged bacterial cell walls; at low concentrations it is bacteriostatic and at high concentrations it disrupts membranes and kills cells [2]. It does not inactivate spores [2]. Because it binds to oral surfaces, it persists in the mouth after rinsing.
It reacts with anionic ingredients such as sodium lauryl sulfate in some toothpastes, which can reduce its activity, and sources suggest leaving a gap after brushing before rinsing [2].

A 2020 crossover study of 36 healthy adults found that seven days of chlorhexidine rinsing changed the salivary microbiome and some saliva and plasma markers compared with placebo [17]. A 2021 report in the Journal of Dentistry examined microbiome effects of the rinse as well [18]. A 2016 study reported stepwise reductions in salivary and plasma nitrite after a dietary nitrate load with increasing strengths of mouthwash [19]. A small randomised study of healthy volunteers taking a proton pump inhibitor, with or without chlorhexidine rinsing, examined oral microbiota translocation to the gut [20].

subs.h: Resistance, blood pressure and other findings
paras: A 2025 systematic review in the British Dental Journal covered 12 studies (seven in vitro, four ex vivo, one in vivo) on mouthwash-induced antimicrobial resistance; it reported higher minimum inhibitory concentrations and more resistance genes in studies of chlorhexidine, cetylpyridinium chloride and hydrogen peroxide, and the authors called the evidence limited.[21] A 2026 scoping review of nine studies on antibacterial mouthwash and blood pressure found significant rises in five and no effect in four, and concluded the evidence was inconclusive.[21] A 2016 nitrate study found that stronger mouthwash lowered salivary and plasma nitrite, which bears on how oral bacteria convert dietary nitrate.[19]

Dental trials include the orthodontic meta-analysis above and a meta-analysis of chlorhexidine as an adjunct to mechanical therapy in chronic periodontitis [3][22]. A 2011 systematic review of 19 articles found that in studies lasting four weeks or more, chlorhexidine gave better plaque control than essential-oil mouthwash, with no significant difference in gingival inflammation [11]. A 2024 meta-analysis of 25 trials with 1,184 participants compared oil pulling with chlorhexidine and other mouthwashes for plaque and gingival indices [12].

Staining has been a trial target in its own right: a 2024 randomised clinical trial reported on reduced staining from a chlorhexidine mouthwash, and a 2021 randomised trial studied an anti-discoloration chlorhexidine formulation [9][10]. A 2024 editorial in Intensive and Critical Care Nursing discussed chlorhexidine mouthwash and halitosis in surgical patients alongside its risks [4].

Hospital studies include Cochrane reviews of oral care in intensive care, mucositis reviews and a 25-patient randomised trial in radiation-induced mucositis [5][6][8][14]. During the COVID-19 pandemic, a report followed saliva viral load at one, two and four hours after chlorhexidine rinsing in two patients, and a randomised trial examined salivary SARS-CoV-2 load after rinsing [23][24].

A 2026 meta-analysis of 26 trials with 1,266 subjects found curcumin and chlorhexidine performed comparably for plaque, gingival and bleeding indices, with chlorhexidine ahead on probing depth and attachment loss in the short term; the authors noted that most of the included studies had a high risk of bias.[21] A 2025 comprehensive review reported that chlorhexidine, essential oils and povidone-iodine reduced gingival inflammation and improved plaque index.[21] A 2026 trial of 60 gingivitis patients found plaque reduction greater with chlorhexidine than with a herbal rinse, while patients rated chlorhexidine higher for taste and freshness.[21]

Chlorhexidine rinses are mentioned in appearance-oriented oral care as a stronger antibacterial option for gum and breath care, with staining of teeth the usual trade-off noted in clinical sources.[2][9] Because brown surface stain is a visible effect, brightening the smile after a course of the rinse is part of the practical discussion; anti-discoloration products were developed for that reason.[9][10] Whether the rinse is sold over the counter or by prescription varies by country and strength.[2]

Alternatives discussed in the literature include essential-oil rinses, which a 2011 review found gave worse plaque control than chlorhexidine in studies of four weeks or longer but with no significant difference in gingival inflammation, cetylpyridinium chloride rinses, which Wikipedia says have less anti-plaque effect than chlorhexidine and may also stain, and oil pulling, which a 2024 meta-analysis compared with chlorhexidine.[11][1][12] Wikipedia notes oil pulling has been little studied and that in one small study it reduced oral bacterial load less than chlorhexidine.[1] Fluoride rinses are used for cavity prevention rather than gum care.[1]

lore.intro: Community discussion of chlorhexidine mouthwash is sparse and mostly about its strength compared with ordinary rinses; the claims below pair what people say with what published sources report.
